items.originalTitle: The dhow builders crafting giant historic ships in India – in pictures
items.author: Frédéric Noy
items.title: The dhow builders crafting giant historic ships in India – in pictures
items.summary: It takes three years for shipbuilders in the 16th-century port of Mandvi to complete a commission, in a trade that is as cultural as it is technical In the 16th century, the port city of Mandvi on India’s west coast was founded by the rulers of the kingdom of Kutch, and quickly established itself as one of the most dynamic ports in the western Indian Ocean. Its strategic geographical position, along the estuary of the Rukmavati River, which flows into the Arabian Sea in the Gulf of Kutch, and mastery of monsoon wind navigation enabled it to become part of vast maritime networks connecting India to the Gulf, the Arabian peninsula and east Africa. Mandvi prospered through trade, exporting cotton textiles, indigo, cereals and handicrafts, while importing dates, pearls, Arabian horses and luxury goods. A stemson, a piece of supporting timber in the bow of a boat, is carved from teak in a Mandvi shipyard under supervision by the master shipwright, or mistri, who designs boats without written plans. items.summary: Thirty years after the roles that made her famous, the star of Three Colours: White and the Before trilogy is busier than ever – as a screenwriter and director. But, she says, a lot of people have tried to keep her down To listen to Julie Delpy talk about her workload is to feel the need for a nap coming on. She is writing six screenplays at the moment that range from dark comedies to thrillers. “I don’t do monoculture,” she says. If her producer hadn’t reined her in, she would be working on five horror film scripts too. The actor, writer and director says she doesn’t sleep well – she can sit at her desk for up to 18 hours, writing “until I run out of steam. I know you could think I’m exaggerating. I’m not. If you look at my computer, you will see how bad it is.” We’re on a video call, Delpy from her home in Los Angeles. She is charming – intense and funny in big black-framed glasses. “I look so weird with this angle on my hair,” she says, of the ceiling light behind her. “Like an angry bald man!”
